claim: Microtubules regulate the turnover of focal adhesions.
source: Microtubules regulate the turnover of adhesion sites
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about microtubule-FA interactions.

claim: Focal adhesions promote cortical microtubule capture and stabilization in their vicinity.
source: focal adhesions promote the cortical microtubule capture and stabilization in their vicinity
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon.

claim: The mechanism underlying focal adhesion-promoted cortical microtubule capture and stabilization was unknown prior to this study.
source: focal adhesions promote the cortical microtubule capture and stabilization in their vicinity, but the underlying mechanism is unknown
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the mechanism was unknown.

claim: Cortical microtubule stabilization sites containing CLASPs, KIF21A, LL5β and liprins are recruited to focal adhesions by KANK1.
source: cortical microtubule stabilization sites containing CLASPs, KIF21A, LL5β and liprins are recruited to focal adhesions by the adaptor protein KANK1
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: KANK1 directly interacts with talin.
source: cortical microtubule stabilization sites containing CLASPs, KIF21A, LL5β and liprins are recruited to focal adhesions by the adaptor protein KANK1, which directly interacts with the major adhesion component, talin
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by pull-down assays and structural studies.

claim: The KN domain in KANK1 is conserved.
source: the conserved KN domain in KANK1 binds to the talin rod domain R7
evidence: The abstract describes the KN domain as conserved.

claim: The KN domain in KANK1 binds to the talin rod domain R7.
source: the conserved KN domain in KANK1 binds to the talin rod domain R7
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through structural studies.

claim: A single point mutation in talin disrupts KANK1 binding but not the talin function in adhesion.
source: Perturbation of this interaction, including a single point mutation in talin, which disrupts KANK1 binding but not the talin function in adhesion, abrogates the association of microtubule-stabilizing complexes with focal adhesions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally with the G1404L mutation.

claim: Perturbation of the talin-KANK1 interaction abrogates the association of microtubule-stabilizing complexes with focal adhesions.
source: Perturbation of this interaction, including a single point mutation in talin, which disrupts KANK1 binding but not the talin function in adhesion, abrogates the association of microtubule-stabilizing complexes with focal adhesions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: The talin-KANK1 interaction links two macromolecular assemblies that control cortical attachment of actin fibers and microtubules.
source: We propose that the talin-KANK1 interaction links the two macromolecular assemblies that control cortical attachment of actin fibers and microtubules.
evidence: This is the main conclusion proposed in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: Talin is a ~2500 amino acid dimeric protein.
source: One of the major components of FAs is talin, a ~2500 amino acid dimeric protein
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Talin plays a key role in adhesion formation by activating integrins.
source: talin, a ~2500 amino acid dimeric protein, which plays a key role in adhesion formation by activating integrins (Anthis et al., 2009)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: Talin couples integrins to cytoskeletal actin.
source: which plays a key role in adhesion formation by activating integrins (Anthis et al., 2009), coupling them to cytoskeletal actin (Atherton et al., 2015)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: Talin regulates adhesion dynamics.
source: regulating adhesion dynamics and recruiting different structural and signaling molecules (Calderwood et al., 2013; Gardel et al., 2010; Wehrle-Haller, 2012)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: Talin recruits different structural and signaling molecules.
source: regulating adhesion dynamics and recruiting different structural and signaling molecules (Calderwood et al., 2013; Gardel et al., 2010; Wehrle-Haller, 2012)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: Microtubules play an important role in adhesion by regulating FA turnover.
source: While the major cytoskeletal element associated with FAs is actin, microtubules also play an important role in adhesion by regulating the FA turnover (Akhmanova et al., 2009; Byron et al., 2015; Kaverina et al., 1999, 1998; Krylyshkina et al., 2003; Small and Kaverina, 2003; Stehbens and Wittmann, 2012; Yue et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from multiple literature sources.

claim: Microtubule-FA cross-talk strongly depends on the activation state of integrins.
source: The recent proteomics work showed that microtubule-FA cross-talk strongly depends on the activation state of the integrins (Byron et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from a specific study.

claim: Microtubules can affect adhesions by serving as tracks for delivery of exocytotic carriers.
source: Microtubules can affect adhesions by serving as tracks for delivery of exocytotic carriers (Stehbens et al., 2014)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: Microtubules can affect adhesions by controlling endocytosis required for adhesion disassembly.
source: by controlling endocytosis required for adhesion disassembly (Ezratty et al., 2005; Theisen et al., 2012)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: Microtubules can affect adhesions by regulating the local activity of signaling molecules such as Rho GTPases.
source: by regulating the local activity of signaling molecules such as Rho GTPases (for review, see [Kaverina and Straube, 2011; Stehbens and Wittmann, 2012])
evidence: This is cited knowledge from review articles.

claim: Microtubules interact with plasma membrane sites that surround FAs rather than directly with FAs.
source: In contrast to actin, which is directly coupled to FAs, microtubules interact with the plasma membrane sites that surround FAs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: CLASP1/2 are microtubule plus end tracking proteins implicated in microtubule attachment and stabilization in the vicinity of FAs.
source: A number of proteins have been implicated in microtubule attachment and stabilization in the vicinity of FAs. Among them are the microtubule plus end tracking proteins (+TIPs) CLASP1/2
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: MACF1/ACF7 is a spectraplakin implicated in microtubule attachment and stabilization in the vicinity of FAs.
source: the spectraplakin MACF1/ACF7, which are targeted to microtubule tips by EB1
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: CLASPs and MACF1/ACF7 are targeted to microtubule tips by EB1.
source: the microtubule plus end tracking proteins (+TIPs) CLASP1/2 and the spectraplakin MACF1/ACF7, which are targeted to microtubule tips by EB1
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: EB2 binds to MAP4K4.
source: a homologue of EB1, EB2, which binds to mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase kinase kinase 4 (MAP4K4) (Drabek et al., 2006; Honnappa et al., 2009; Kodama et al., 2003; Mimori-Kiyosue et al., 2005)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: The interaction of CLASPs with the cell cortex depends on LL5β.
source: The interaction of CLASPs with the cell cortex depends on the phosphatidylinositol 3, 4, 5-trisphosphate (PIP3)-interacting protein LL5β, to which CLASPs bind directly
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: CLASPs bind directly to LL5β.
source: The interaction of CLASPs with the cell cortex depends on the phosphatidylinositol 3, 4, 5-trisphosphate (PIP3)-interacting protein LL5β, to which CLASPs bind directly
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: The interaction of CLASPs with the cell cortex is partly regulated by PI-3 kinase activity.
source: The interaction of CLASPs with the cell cortex depends on the phosphatidylinositol 3, 4, 5-trisphosphate (PIP3)-interacting protein LL5β, to which CLASPs bind directly, and is partly regulated by PI-3 kinase activity (Lansbergen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: Liprin-α1, liprin-β1, ELKS/ERC1, and KIF21A are components of cortical microtubule stabilization complexes.
source: Other components of the same cortical assembly are the scaffolding proteins liprin-α1 and β1, a coiled-coil adaptor ELKS/ERC1, and the kinesin-4 KIF21A (Lansbergen et al., 2006; van der Vaart et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: Liprins and ELKS are best known for their role in organizing presynaptic secretory sites.
source: Both liprins and ELKS are best known for their role in organizing presynaptic secretory sites (Hida and Ohtsuka, 2010; Spangler and Hoogenraad, 2007)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: ELKS is required for efficient constitutive exocytosis in HeLa cells.
source: in agreement with this function, ELKS is required for efficient constitutive exocytosis in HeLa cells (Grigoriev et al., 2007, 2011)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: LL5β, liprins and ELKS form micrometer-sized cortical patch-like structures.
source: LL5β, liprins and ELKS form micrometer-sized cortical patch-like structures, which will be termed here cortical microtubule stabilization complexes, or CMSCs
evidence: This is stated based on cited knowledge.

claim: CMSCs are strongly enriched at the leading cell edges.
source: The CMSCs are strongly enriched at the leading cell edges, where they localize in close proximity of FAs but do not overlap with them ([Lansbergen et al., 2006; van der Vaart et al., 2013], reviewed in [Astro and de Curtis, 2015])
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: CMSCs localize in close proximity of FAs but do not overlap with them.
source: The CMSCs are strongly enriched at the leading cell edges, where they localize in close proximity of FAs but do not overlap with them ([Lansbergen et al., 2006; van der Vaart et al., 2013], reviewed in [Astro and de Curtis, 2015])
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: CMSC patches can remain relatively stable for tens of minutes.
source: The CMSC 'patches' can remain relatively stable for tens of minutes, while their individual components are dynamic and exchange with different, characteristic turnover rates (van der Vaart et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: In migrating keratinocytes, LL5β and CLASPs accumulate around FAs and promote their disassembly by targeting the exocytosis of matrix metalloproteases to FA vicinity.
source: In migrating keratinocytes, LL5β and CLASPs accumulate around FAs and promote their disassembly by targeting the exocytosis of matrix metalloproteases to FA vicinity (Stehbens et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: Liprin-α1, LL5α/β and ELKS localize to protrusions of human breast cancer cells and are required for efficient cell migration and FA turnover.
source: Furthermore, liprin-α1, LL5α/β and ELKS localize to protrusions of human breast cancer cells and are required for efficient cell migration and FA turnover (Astro et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: In polarized epithelial cells, LL5β and CLASPs are found in the proximity of the basal membrane, and this localization is controlled by the integrin activation state.
source: In polarized epithelial cells, LL5β and CLASPs are found in the proximity of the basal membrane, and this localization is controlled by the integrin activation state (Hotta et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: CLASP and LL5-mediated anchoring of MTs to the basal cortex plays a role during chicken embryonic development by preventing epithelial-mesenchymal transition of epiblast cells.
source: CLASP and LL5-mediated anchoring of MTs to the basal cortex also plays a role during chicken embryonic development, where it prevents the epithelial-mesenchymal transition of epiblast cells (Nakaya et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: LL5β, CLASPs and ELKS concentrate at podosomes.
source: LL5β, CLASPs and ELKS were also shown to concentrate at podosomes, actin-rich structures, which can remodel the extracellular matrix (Proszynski and Sanes, 2013).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: LL5β-containing podosome-like structures are formed at neuromuscular junctions.
source: Interestingly, LL5β-containing podosome-like structures are also formed at neuromuscular junctions (Kishi et al., 2005; Proszynski et al., 2009; Proszynski and Sanes, 2013)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: Complexes of LL5β and CLASPs capture microtubule plus ends and promote delivery of acetylcholine receptors.
source: the complexes of LL5β and CLASPs were shown to capture microtubule plus ends and promote delivery of acetylcholine receptors (Basu et al., 2015, 2014; Schmidt et al., 2012)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: The mechanism underlying specific targeting of CMSCs to integrin adhesion sites was elusive prior to this study.
source: While the roles of CMSCs in migrating cells and in tissues are becoming increasingly clear, the mechanism underlying their specific targeting to integrin adhesion sites remains elusive.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a knowledge gap.

claim: Liprin-β1 interacts with KANK1.
source: Recently, we found that liprin-β1 interacts with KANK1 (van der Vaart et al., 2013)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from previous work by the authors.

claim: KANK proteins were proposed to act as tumor suppressors and regulators of cell polarity and migration through Rho GTPase signaling.
source: one of the four members of the KANK family of proteins, which were proposed to act as tumor suppressors and regulators of cell polarity and migration through Rho GTPase signaling (Gee et al., 2015; Kakinuma et al., 2008, 2009; Li et al., 2011; Roy et al., 2009)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: KANK1 recruits KIF21A to CMSCs.
source: KANK1 recruits the kinesin-4 KIF21A to CMSCs, which inhibits microtubule polymerization and prevents microtubule overgrowth at the cell edge (Kakinuma and Kiyama, 2009; van der Vaart et al., 2013)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: KIF21A inhibits microtubule polymerization and prevents microtubule overgrowth at the cell edge.
source: KANK1 recruits the kinesin-4 KIF21A to CMSCs, which inhibits microtubule polymerization and prevents microtubule overgrowth at the cell edge (Kakinuma and Kiyama, 2009; van der Vaart et al., 2013)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: KANK1 participates in clustering of CMSC components.
source: Furthermore, KANK1 participates in clustering of the other CMSC components (van der Vaart et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from previous work by the authors.

claim: Endogenous KANK1 colocalizes with LL5β, liprins and KIF21A in cortical patches that are closely apposed to, but do not overlap with FAs.
source: Our previous work showed that the endogenous KANK1 colocalizes with LL5β, liprins and KIF21A in cortical patches that are closely apposed to, but do not overlap with FAs (van der Vaart et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work and confirmed in this study.

claim: The colocalization of endogenous KANK1 with LL5β, liprins and KIF21A in cortical patches near FAs was confirmed in HeLa cells and HaCaT immortal keratinocyte cell line.
source: We confirmed these results both in HeLa cells and the HaCaT immortal keratinocyte cell line, in which CMSC components CLASPs and LL5β were previously shown to strongly cluster around FAs and regulate their turnover during cell migration (Stehbens et al., 2014) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Inhibition of myosin-II with blebbistatin causes FA disassembly and a strong reduction in clustering of CMSC components at the cell periphery.
source: Inhibition of myosin-II with blebbistatin, which reduces tension on the actin fibers and affects the activation state of FA molecules, such as integrins and talin (Parsons et al., 2010), caused not only FA disassembly but also a strong reduction in clustering of CMSC components at the cell periphery (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B), as described previously (Stehbens et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Partial inhibition of contractility using ROCK1 inhibitor Y-27632 does not affect the number of FAs but reduces their size.
source: To investigate this effect in more detail, we partially inhibited contractility using a Rho-associated protein kinase 1 (ROCK1) inhibitor, Y-27632 (Oakes et al., 2012). In these conditions, the number of FAs was not affected although their size was reduced (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–E.

claim: ROCK1 inhibitor treatment is sufficient to diminish CMSC clustering at the cell edge.
source: This treatment was sufficient to diminish CMSC clustering at the cell edge (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,F.

claim: ROCK1 inhibitor treatment causes a very significant increase in the overlap of KANK1 with FA adhesion markers.
source: Interestingly, at the same time we observed a very significant increase in the overlap of KANK1 with FA adhesion markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,G.

claim: Live imaging shows gradual redistribution of KANK1 into areas occupied by FAs upon ROCK1 inhibitor-induced attenuation of contractility.
source: Live imaging of KANK1 together with the FA marker paxillin showed a gradual redistribution of KANK1 into the areas occupied by FAs upon ROCK1 inhibitor-induced attenuation of contractility (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H, Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2H and Video 1.

claim: The organization of CMSCs at the cell cortex might be controlled by interactions with tension-sensitive components of FAs.
source: These data indicate that the organization of CMSCs at the cell cortex might be controlled by interactions with tension-sensitive components of FAs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The KN domain alone strongly and specifically accumulates within FAs.
source: Surprisingly, the KN domain alone strongly and specifically accumulated within FAs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1B.

claim: The Nter fragment of KANK1 shows similar localization to the KN domain.
source: A similar localization was also seen with a somewhat larger N-terminal fragment of KANK1, Nter
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1B.

claim: The Nter-CC1 deletion mutant of KANK1 shows similar localization to the KN domain.
source: as well as the Nter-CC1 deletion mutant, which contained the first, liprin-β1-binding coiled coil region of KANK1 (Figure 1A,B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A,B.

claim: The Nter-CC fragment of KANK1 shows pronounced enrichment at the FA rim.
source: However, an even larger N-terminal part of KANK1, encompassing the whole coiled coil domain (Nter-CC) showed a pronounced enrichment at the FA rim (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A,B.

claim: The KANK1 △ANKR mutant is completely excluded from FAs but accumulates in their immediate vicinity.
source: The KANK1 deletion mutant missing only the C-terminal ankyrin repeat domain (△ANKR) was completely excluded from FAs but accumulated in their immediate vicinity, similar to the full-length KANK1 (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A,B.

claim: The KANK1 △CC mutant shows tight ring-like localization at the outer rim of FAs.
source: A tight ring-like localization at the outer rim of FAs was also observed with a KANK1 mutant, which completely missed the coiled coil region but contained the ankyrin repeat domain (△CC)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1B.

claim: The KANK1 mutant missing the KN domain shows no accumulation around FAs.
source: while the mutant which missed just the KN domain showed no accumulation around FAs (Figure 1A,B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A,B.

claim: GFP-KN-LacZ fusion accumulates inside and not around FAs.
source: To test whether the exclusion of larger KANK1 fragments from the FA core was simply due to the protein size, we fused GFP-tagged KN domain to the bacterial protein β-D-galactosidase (LacZ), but found that this fusion accumulated inside and not around FAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Features other than protein size determine the specific localization of KANK1 to the FA rim.
source: Since GFP-KN-LacZ and GFP-KANK1-△ANKRD have a similar size (1336 and 1400 amino acids, respectively), but one accumulates inside FAs, while the other is excluded to their periphery, this result suggests that features other than the mere protein size determine the specific localization of KANK1 to the FA rim.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The KN domain of KANK1 has an affinity for FAs.
source: We conclude that the KN domain of KANK1 has an affinity for FAs, but the presence of additional KANK1 sequences prevents the accumulation of the protein inside FAs and instead leads to the accumulation of KANK1 at the FA periphery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the deletion mapping experiments.

claim: The presence of additional KANK1 sequences prevents the accumulation of the protein inside FAs and leads to accumulation at the FA periphery.
source: We conclude that the KN domain of KANK1 has an affinity for FAs, but the presence of additional KANK1 sequences prevents the accumulation of the protein inside FAs and instead leads to the accumulation of KANK1 at the FA periphery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the deletion mapping experiments.

claim: Talin1 was identified among the strongest hits in mass spectrometry analysis of KANK1 binding partners.
source: In addition to the already known binding partners of KANK1, such as KIF21A, liprins and LL5β, we identified talin1 among the strongest hits (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1C showing mass spectrometry data.

claim: Talin2 was detected in a pull down with the KANK1 N-terminus though not with the full-length protein.
source: Talin2 was also detected in a pull down with the KANK1 N-terminus though not with the full-length protein (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1C.

claim: The interaction between KANK1 and talin1 was confirmed by Western blotting.
source: The interaction between KANK1 and talin1 was confirmed by Western blotting
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1D.

claim: The talin1-binding region of KANK1 encompasses the KN domain.
source: subsequent deletion mapping showed that the talin1-binding region of KANK1 encompasses the KN domain (Figure 1A,D)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A,D.

claim: Liprin-β1 binds to the N-terminal part of the coiled coil domain of KANK1.
source: while liprin-β1 binds to the N-terminal part of the coiled coil domain, as shown previously (van der Vaart et al., 2013)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from previous work by the authors.

claim: The KN domain is predicted to form a helix.
source: Sequence analysis of the KN domain showed that it is predicted to form a helix
evidence: This is stated based on sequence analysis.

claim: The KN domain contains a completely conserved leucine aspartic acid-motif (LD-motif).
source: Sequence analysis of the KN domain showed that it is predicted to form a helix and contains a completely conserved leucine aspartic acid-motif (LD-motif) (Alam et al., 2014; Zacharchenko et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated based on sequence analysis with citations.

claim: The LD-motifs in RIAM, DLC1 and Paxillin have been identified as talin-binding sites that interact with talin via a helix addition mechanism.
source: The LD-motifs in RIAM (Goult et al., 2013), DLC1 and Paxillin (Zacharchenko et al., 2016) have recently been identified as talin-binding sites that all interact with talin via a helix addition mechanism.
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: Alignment of the KN domain of KANK with the LD-motif of DLC1, RIAM and Paxillin revealed that the hydrophobic residues that mediate interaction with talin are present in the KN domain.
source: Alignment of the KN domain of KANK with the LD-motif of DLC1, RIAM and Paxillin (Zacharchenko et al., 2016) revealed that the hydrophobic residues that mediate interaction with talin are present in the KN domain (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1E showing sequence alignment.

claim: The KANK1-binding site of talin1 was mapped to the central region of the talin rod, comprising the R7-R8 domains.
source: Using deletion analysis, we mapped the KANK1-binding site of talin1 to the central region of the talin rod, comprising the R7-R8 domains (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1F.

claim: The R7-R8 region of talin is unique as the 4-helix bundle R8 is inserted into a loop of the 5-helix bundle R7.
source: This R7-R8 region of talin is unique (Gingras et al., 2010), as the 4-helix bundle R8 is inserted into a loop of the 5-helix bundle R7, and thus protrudes from the linear chain of 5-helix bundles of the talin rod (Figures 1F, 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation and supported by Figures 1F and 2A.

claim: The R8 domain serves as a binding hub for numerous proteins including vinculin, synemin and actin.
source: This R8 domain serves as a binding hub for numerous proteins including vinculin, synemin and actin (Calderwood et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: R8 contains a prototypic recognition site for LD-motif proteins, including DLC1, Paxillin and RIAM.
source: R8 also contains a prototypic recognition site for LD-motif proteins, including DLC1 (Figure 2B), Paxillin and RIAM (Zacharchenko et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Deletion mapping revealed that KANK1 binds to the talin1 rod domain R7.
source: However, deletion mapping revealed that KANK1 in fact binds to the talin1 rod domain R7 (Figure 1F,G), suggesting that KANK1 interacts with a novel binding site on talin1.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1F,G.

claim: KANK1 interacts with a novel binding site on talin1.
source: However, deletion mapping revealed that KANK1 in fact binds to the talin1 rod domain R7 (Figure 1F,G), suggesting that KANK1 interacts with a novel binding site on talin1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the deletion mapping results.

claim: Addition of KANK1(30–60) peptide to 15N-labeled talin1 R7-R8 resulted in large spectral changes in NMR.
source: The addition of the KANK1(30–60) peptide resulted in large spectral changes (Figure 2C), most of which were in the slow exchange regime on the NMR timescale indicative of a tight interaction.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2C showing NMR spectra.

claim: The signals that shifted upon addition of KANK1(30–60) mapped largely onto the R7 domain with only small progressive shift changes on R8.
source: In agreement with the pull down data, the signals that shifted in slow exchange upon the addition of KANK1(30–60) mapped largely onto the R7 domain with only small progressive shift changes evident on R8.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on NMR chemical shift mapping.

claim: Addition of KANK1(30–60) to R8 domain induced small chemical shift changes indicative of a weak interaction.
source: Addition of KANK1(30–60) induced small chemical shift changes on the R8 domain indicative of a weak interaction (most likely due to the interaction of LD with the LD-recognition box on R8).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on NMR experiments.

claim: Addition of KANK1(30–60) to R7 induced large spectral changes indicative of slow-exchange and confirms a high affinity interaction.
source: However, the addition of a 0.5 molar ratio of KANK1(30–60) to R7 induced large spectral changes with many of the peaks displaying two locations, corresponding to the free peak position and the bound peak position. This is indicative of slow-exchange and confirms a high affinity interaction between R7 and KANK1.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on NMR experiments.

claim: The KN peptide is the first identified ligand for the R7 domain.
source: The KN peptide is the first identified ligand for the R7 domain.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the NMR experiments.

claim: Chemical shift changes mapped predominantly onto one face of R7, comprised of helices 2 and 5 of the 5-helix bundle (talin rod helices 29 and 36).
source: The chemical shift changes mapped predominantly onto one face of R7, comprised of helices 2 and 5 of the 5-helix bundle (talin rod helices 29 and 36), as shown in Figure 2D–E.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2D–E.

claim: The surface of α2 and α5 on R7 forms a hydrophobic groove that the KANK1 helix docks into.
source: The surface of α2 and α5 on R7 forms a hydrophobic groove that the KANK1 helix docks into.
evidence: This is stated based on structural analysis.

claim: W1630 and Y1389 hold the two helices of the KANK1 binding site apart by ~8Å.
source: A striking feature of this KANK1 binding surface is that the two helices are held apart by the conserved aromatic residues, W1630 at the end of α5 and Y1389 at the end of α2 (Figure 2B,E). W1630 and Y1389 thus essentially serve as molecular rulers, separating helices α2 and α5 by ~8Å (compared with ~5–6Å for the other bundles in R7-R8).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2B,E.

claim: Small side chains on the inner helical faces create two conserved pockets midway along the hydrophobic groove of the KANK1-binding site.
source: The spacing between the two helices is enhanced further as the residues on the inner helical faces, S1400, G1404, S1411 on α2 and S1637 and S1641 on α5, have small side chains which have the effect of creating two conserved pockets midway along the hydrophobic groove of the KANK1-binding site (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2E.

claim: The talin-binding site on KANK1 contains a double LD-motif, LDLD.
source: The talin-binding site on KANK1 is unusual as it contains a double LD-motif, LDLD.
evidence: This is stated based on sequence analysis.

claim: K1401 and R1652 are positioned on either side of the LD-recognition box to engage either one, or both, of the aspartic residues.
source: The structure of R7 revealed a potential LD-recognition box with the positive charges, K1401 and R1652 positioned on either side to engage either one, or both, of the aspartic residues.
evidence: This is stated based on structural analysis.

claim: HADDOCK docking analysis indicated that the KANK-LD helix can pack against the sides of α2 and α5.
source: Using the docking program HADDOCK (van Zundert et al., 2016), we sought to generate a structural model of the KANK1/R7 complex, using the chemical shift mapping on R7 and a model of KANK1(30–60) as a helix (created by threading the KANK1 sequence onto the DLC1 LD-motif helix). This analysis indicated that the KANK-LD helix can indeed pack against the sides of α2 and α5 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2E showing the structural model.

claim: All docking models positioned the bulky aromatic residue Y48 in KANK1 in the hydrophobic pocket created by G1404.
source: Interestingly, all of the models, irrespective of which way the KANK1 helix ran along the surface, positioned the bulky aromatic residue, Y48 in KANK1, in the hydrophobic pocket created by G1404.
evidence: This is stated based on docking analysis.

claim: Mutation of G1404 to a bulky hydrophobic residue might block KANK1 binding by preventing Y48 engagement.
source: This raised the possibility that mutation of G1404 to a bulky hydrophobic residue might block KANK1 binding by preventing Y48 engagement.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural model.

claim: S1641 has been shown to be phosphorylated in vivo.
source: We also noticed that S1641, one of the small residues that create the pocket, has been shown to be phosphorylated in vivo (Ratnikov et al., 2005)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: S1641 might have a regulatory function in the KANK1-talin1 interaction.
source: We also noticed that S1641, one of the small residues that create the pocket, has been shown to be phosphorylated in vivo (Ratnikov et al., 2005) and might have a regulatory function in the KANK1-talin1 interaction.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural analysis and known phosphorylation.

claim: The KANK1-4A mutant abolished binding to talin.
source: The KANK1-4A mutant abolished binding to talin (Figure 2C,F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2C,F showing NMR and fluorescence polarization data.

claim: The S1641E mutant had only a small effect on binding.
source: The S1641E mutant had only a small effect on binding (Figure 2G)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2G.

claim: Talin1 phosphorylation might not play a major role in modulating the interaction with KANK1, or the S-E mutation is not a good phosphomimetic.
source: suggesting that either talin1 phosphorylation does not play a major role in modulating the interaction with KANK1 or that the S-E mutation is not a good phosphomimetic, possibly because phosphorylation might also affect helix formation integrity, an effect not mimicked by a single aspartate residue.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Both the W1630A and the G1404L mutants abolished binding of KANK1 to talin R7.
source: However, strikingly, both the W1630A and the G1404L mutants abolished binding of KANK1 to talin R7 (Figure 2G), confirming the validity of our model.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2G showing fluorescence polarization data.

claim: The KN-R7 interaction is conserved in talin2 and KANK2.
source: Finally, we also tested whether the KN-R7 interaction is conserved in talin2 and KANK2, and found that this was indeed the case (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The conserved KN domain of KANKs is a talin-binding site.
source: We conclude that the conserved KN domain of KANKs is a talin-binding site.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and biochemical experiments.

claim: The 4A mutation reduced the interaction of the full-length KANK1 with talin1 in a pull-down assay.
source: As could be expected based on the binding experiments with purified protein fragments, the 4A mutation reduced the interaction of the full-length KANK1 with talin1 in a pull-down assay (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3A.

claim: An even stronger reduction in talin1 binding was observed when KANK-△CC or the KN alone were tested.
source: An even stronger reduction was observed when KANK-△CC or the KN alone were tested (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3A.

claim: The introduction of the G1404L mutation abrogated the interaction of full-length talin1 or its R7 fragment with full-length KANK1.
source: Furthermore, the introduction of the G1404L mutation abrogated the interaction of full-length talin1 or its R7 fragment with full-length KANK1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3B.

claim: Wild type GFP-KANK1 strongly accumulated in cortical patches that were tightly clustered around FAs.
source: Total Internal Reflection Fluorescence Microscopy (TIRFM)-based live imaging showed that, consistent with our previous results, the GFP-tagged wild type KANK1 strongly accumulated in cortical patches that were tightly clustered around FAs (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3C,D.

claim: The KANK1-△CC mutant showed highly specific ring-like accumulations at the rims of FAs.
source: The KANK1-△CC mutant, which lacked the liprin-β1-binding site but contained an intact KN motif, showed highly specific ring-like accumulations at the rims of FAs (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3C,D.

claim: KANK1-4A was not clustered around FAs but was dispersed over the cell cortex.
source: In contrast, KANK1-4A was not clustered anymore around FAs but was dispersed over the cell cortex (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3C,D.

claim: The KANK1-△CC-4A mutant and the KN-4A mutant were completely diffuse.
source: The KANK1-△CC-4A mutant, lacking both the liprin-β1 and the talin-binding sites, and the KN-4A mutant were completely diffuse (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3C,D.

claim: The GFP-talin1-G1404L mutant could fully support cell attachment and spreading.
source: The GFP-talin1-G1404L mutant could fully support cell attachment and spreading, although the cell area was slightly increased compared to cells rescued with the wild type GFP-talin1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: The number and size of focal adhesions were not significantly different between cells rescued with wild type talin1 or its G1404L mutant.
source: The number and size of focal adhesions were not significantly different between the cells rescued with the wild type talin1 or its G1404L mutant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G), indicating that the mutant is functional in supporting FA formation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: In cells expressing wild-type talin1, KANK1 was prominently clustered around FAs, but was dispersed over the plasma membrane in cells expressing talin1-G1404L.
source: Strikingly, while in cells expressing the wild-type talin1, KANK1 was prominently clustered around FAs, it was dispersed over the plasma membrane in cells expressing talin1-G1404L (Figure 3E,F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Perturbing the KANK1-talin interaction abrogates KANK1 association with FAs.
source: We conclude that perturbing the KANK1-talin interaction, including the use of a single point mutation in the ~2500 amino acid long talin1 protein, which does not interfere with the talin function in FA formation, abrogates KANK1 association with FAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Co-depletion of KANK1 and KANK2 abolished clustering of CMSC components LL5β and KIF21A at the cell edge.
source: Co-depletion of KANK1 and KANK2 abolished clustering of CMSC components, such as LL5β and KIF21A at the cell edge (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4B,C.

claim: Wild type GFP-KANK1 could rescue cortical clustering of LL5β and KIF21A in KANK1 and KANK2-depleted cells.
source: Wild type GFP-KANK1 could rescue cortical clustering of these proteins in KANK1 and KANK2-depleted cells (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4B,C.

claim: The KANK1-4A mutant, the KANK1-△CC mutant and the KANK1 version bearing both mutations could not rescue cortical clustering of LL5β and KIF21A.
source: However, this was not the case for the KANK1-4A mutant, the KANK1-△CC mutant or the KANK1 version bearing both mutations (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4B,C.

claim: The dispersed puncta of the KANK1-4A mutant still colocalized with LL5β.
source: Importantly, the dispersed puncta of the KANK1-4A mutant still colocalized with LL5β, as the binding to liprin-β1 was intact in this mutant (Figure 3A, Figure 4B,C)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3A and Figure 4B,C.

claim: The FA-associated rings of KANK1-△CC showed a mutually exclusive localization with LL5β.
source: while the FA-associated rings of KANK1-△CC, the mutant deficient in liprin-β1 binding, showed a mutually exclusive localization with LL5β (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4B.

claim: KIF21A could still colocalize with KANK1-△CC at FA rims.
source: In contrast, KIF21A, which binds to the ankyrin repeat domain of KANK1, could still colocalize with KANK1-△CC at FA rims (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4B.

claim: Only the full-length wild type KANK1, but neither the 4A nor △CC mutant could support efficient accumulation of CLASP2 at the peripheral cell cortex in KANK1 and KANK2-depleted cells.
source: Furthermore, only the full-length wild type KANK1, but neither the 4A nor △CC mutant could support efficient accumulation of CLASP2 at the peripheral cell cortex in KANK1 and KANK2-depleted cells (Figure 4D,E)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4D,E.

claim: Cortical recruitment of CLASPs depends on LL5β.
source: in line with the fact that cortical recruitment of CLASPs depends on LL5β (Lansbergen et al., 2006)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: Both LL5β and KIF21A were clustered around FAs in talin1 and talin2-depleted cells rescued with wild type GFP-talin1, but not in cells expressing GFP-talin1-G1404L mutant.
source: Next, we investigated whether disrupting the KANK1-talin1 interaction from the talin1 side would affect also CMSC localization and found that this was indeed the case: both LL5β and KIF21A were clustered around FAs in talin1 and talin2-depleted cells rescued with the wild type GFP-talin1, but not in the cells expressing the GFP-talin1-G1404L mutant, deficient in KANK1 binding (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4F,G.

claim: KANK1-△CC could not support proper clustering of CMSC components at the cell edge in spite of its tight accumulation at the FA rims.
source: Our data showed that KANK1-△CC could not support proper clustering of CMSC components at the cell edge in spite of its tight accumulation at the FA rims.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental observations.

claim: In addition to binding to talin1, the localization of CMSC clusters depends on the KANK1-liprin-β1 connection.
source: These data indicate that in addition to binding to talin1, the localization of CMSC clusters depends on the KANK1-liprin-β1 connection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The overexpressed coiled coil region of KANK1 (CC1) acted as a dominant negative, which suppressed accumulation of LL5β at the cell periphery.
source: This notion is supported by the observation that the overexpressed coiled coil region of KANK1 (CC1), which can compete for liprin-β1 binding but cannot interact with talin1, acted as a very potent dominant negative, which suppressed accumulation of LL5β at the cell periphery (Figure 4H,I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4H,I.

claim: The core CMSC protein LL5β as well as the microtubule-binding CMSC components KIF21A and CLASP2 depend on the KANK1 interaction with both talin1 and liprin-β1 for their efficient clustering in the vicinity of focal adhesions at the cell periphery.
source: We conclude that the core CMSC protein LL5β as well as the microtubule-binding CMSC components KIF21A and CLASP2 depend on the KANK1 interaction with both talin1 and liprin-β1 for their efficient clustering in the vicinity of focal adhesions at the cell periphery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: In HeLa cells, microtubules grow rapidly in the central parts of the cell.
source: In this cell line, microtubules grow rapidly in the central parts of the cell
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about HeLa cells.

claim: At the cell margin in HeLa cells, microtubule plus ends are tethered to the cortex and display persistent but slow growth.
source: while at the cell margin, where CMSCs cluster in the vicinity of peripheral FAs, microtubule plus ends are tethered to the cortex and display persistent but slow growth due to the combined action of several types of microtubule regulators, including CLASPs, spectraplakins and KIF21A (Drabek et al., 2006; Mimori-Kiyosue et al., 2005; van der Vaart et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: This type of regulation prevents microtubule overgrowth at the cell edge and results in an orderly arrangement of microtubule plus ends perpendicular to the cell margin.
source: This type of regulation prevents microtubule overgrowth at the cell edge and results in an orderly arrangement of microtubule plus ends perpendicular to the cell margin (van der Vaart et al., 2013) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: In cells with perturbed CMSCs, microtubule plus ends at the cell periphery become disorganized: the velocity of their growth at the cell margin increases, and their orientation becomes parallel instead of perpendicular to the cell edge.
source: In cells with perturbed CMSCs, microtubule plus ends at the cell periphery become disorganized: the velocity of their growth at the cell margin increases, and their orientation becomes parallel instead of being perpendicular to the cell edge (van der Vaart et al., 2013) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: In KANK1/2 depleted cells rescued with wild-type GFP-KANK1, microtubule plus end growth velocity was almost 2.5 times slower at the cell margin compared to the central part of the cell.
source: Using live cell imaging of the microtubule plus end marker EB3-mRFP in KANK1/2 depleted cells rescued with the wild-type GFP-KANK1, we could indeed show that microtubule plus end growth velocity was almost 2.5 times slower at the cell margin compared to the central part of the cell
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5B–E.

claim: In KANK1/2 depleted cells rescued with wild-type GFP-KANK1, the majority of microtubules at the cell margin grew at a 60–80° angle to the cell edge.
source: and the majority of microtubules at the cell margin grew at a 60–80° angle to the cell edge (Figure 5B–E)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5B–E.

claim: In KANK1/2 depleted cells expressing KANK1 mutants, the velocity of microtubule growth in central cell regions was not affected, but the growth rate at the cell periphery increased, and microtubules were growing at oblique angles to the cell margin.
source: In the KANK1/2 depleted cells expressing KANK1 mutants, the velocity of microtubule growth in central cell regions was not affected, but the growth rate at the cell periphery increased, and microtubules were growing at oblique angles to the cell margin (Figure 5B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5B–E.

claim: The increase of the microtubule growth rate observed with the GFP-KANK1-ΔCC mutant was less strong than with the two 4A mutants.
source: The increase of the microtubule growth rate observed with the GFP-KANK1-ΔCC mutant was less strong than with the two 4A mutants (Figure 5B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5B–E.

claim: GFP-KANK1-ΔCC was strongly clustered at FA rims and could still recruit some KIF21A through its ankyrin repeat domain.
source: This can be explained by the fact that GFP-KANK1-ΔCC was strongly clustered at FA rims (Figure 3C, Figure 5B), and, through its ankyrin repeat domain, could still recruit some KIF21A, a potent microtubule polymerization inhibitor (van der Vaart et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an explanation provided in the text based on previous observations.

claim: In GFP-talin1-expressing cells, microtubule growth at the cell edge was three fold slower than in the cell center.
source: The results with rescue of talin1 and talin2 co-depletion with GFP-talin1 or its G1404L mutant fully supported the conclusions obtained with the KANK1-4A mutant: while in GFP-talin1-expressing cells microtubule growth at the cell edge was three fold slower than in the cell center
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5F–I.

claim: In GFP-talin1-G1404L expressing cells, only a 1.5 fold difference in microtubule growth rate was observed between cell center and edge.
source: only a 1.5 fold difference was observed in GFP-talin1-G1404L expressing cells
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5F–I.

claim: In GFP-talin1-G1404L expressing cells, the proportion of microtubules growing parallel rather than perpendicular to the cell edge greatly increased.
source: and the proportion of microtubules growing parallel rather than perpendicular to the cell edge greatly increased (Figure 5F–I)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5F–I.

claim: A single point mutation in talin1, which does not interfere with FA formation, is sufficient to perturb CMSC clustering and induce microtubule disorganization in the vicinity of peripheral FAs.
source: We conclude that a single point mutation in talin1, which does not interfere with FA formation, is sufficient to perturb CMSC clustering and, as a consequence, induce microtubule disorganization in the vicinity of peripheral FAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The function of KANK1-talin binding is likely to be conserved in the animal kingdom.
source: This function is likely to be conserved in the animal kingdom, as the KANK orthologue in C. elegans, Vab-19, in conjunction with integrins, plays important roles in a dynamic cell-extracellular matrix adhesion developmental process (Ihara et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited knowledge about C. elegans.

claim: The exact impact of KANK1-talin binding likely depends on the specific system.
source: The exact impact of KANK1-talin binding likely depends on the specific system, as the loss of KANK proteins was shown to reduce motility of HeLa cells and podocytes (Gee et al., 2015; Li et al., 2011), but promote insulin-dependent cell migration in HEK293 cells (Kakinuma et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on cited knowledge from different studies.

claim: Reducing contractility with a ROCK1 inhibitor causes an increase in overlap of KANK1 with FA markers.
source: Interestingly, we found that reducing contractility with a ROCK1 inhibitor caused an increase in overlap of KANK1 with FA markers, suggesting that the interaction between KANK1 and talin might be mechanosensitive.
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations.

claim: The interaction between KANK1 and talin might be mechanosensitive.
source: Interestingly, we found that reducing contractility with a ROCK1 inhibitor caused an increase in overlap of KANK1 with FA markers, suggesting that the interaction between KANK1 and talin might be mechanosensitive.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on experimental observations.

claim: Full length KANK1 can efficiently interact only with talin molecules at the periphery of focal adhesions because they are not fully incorporated into the focal adhesion structure and are thus less stretched.
source: An exciting possibility is that full length KANK1 can efficiently interact only with talin molecules at the periphery of focal adhesions because they are not fully incorporated into the focal adhesion structure and are thus less stretched.
evidence: This is presented as a speculative possibility.

claim: The KANK1 binding site on talin R7 overlaps with the high affinity actin binding site in talin.
source: The KANK1 binding site on talin R7 overlaps with the high affinity actin binding site in talin (which spans R4-R8) (Atherton et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated based on cited knowledge.

claim: Different conformational populations of talin might exist within adhesions and link to different cytoskeletal components.
source: it is possible that different conformational populations of talin exist within adhesions and link to different cytoskeletal components.
evidence: This is presented as a speculative possibility.

claim: The 'core' components of CMSCs are LL5β, liprins and KANKs, which can be recruited to the plasma membrane independently of each other.
source: The 'core' components of these complexes, which can be recruited to the plasma membrane independently of each other, are LL5β (and in some cells, its homologue LL5α), liprins and KANKs (of which KANK1 seems to predominate in HeLa cells) (Astro and de Curtis, 2015; Hotta et al., 2010; Lansbergen et al., 2006; van der Vaart et al., 2013) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated based on cited knowledge and illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: The clustering of CMSC components is mutually dependent and relies on homo- and heterodimerization of liprins α1 and β1, the association between KANK1 and liprin-β1, the scaffolding protein ELKS, and possibly additional interactions.
source: The clustering of CMSC components is mutually dependent and relies on homo- and heterodimerization of liprins α1 and β1, the association between KANK1 and liprin-β1, the scaffolding protein ELKS, which binds to both LL5β and liprin-α1, and possibly additional interactions (Astro and de Curtis, 2015; Lansbergen et al., 2006; van der Vaart et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated based on cited knowledge.

claim: The microtubule-binding proteins CLASPs and KIF21A associate as a second 'layer' with the membrane-bound CMSC-assemblies.
source: while the microtubule-binding proteins, such as CLASPs and KIF21A, seem to associate as a second 'layer' with the membrane-bound CMSC-assemblies (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is stated based on knowledge and illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: The dynamic assemblies of CMSC components are reminiscent of cytoplasmic and nucleoplasmic membrane-unbounded organelles such as P granules and stress granules, the assembly of which has been proposed to be driven by phase transitions.
source: The dynamic assemblies of CMSC components, which are spatially separate from other plasma membrane domains and which rely on multivalent protein-protein interactions, are reminiscent of cytoplasmic and nucleoplasmic membrane-unbounded organelles such as P granules and stress granules, the assembly of which has been proposed to be driven by phase transitions (Astro and de Curtis, 2015; Brangwynne, 2013; Hyman and Simons, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as an analogy with cited knowledge.

claim: By concentrating KANK1 at the FA rims, talin1 helps to 'nucleate' CMSC assembly, which can then propagate to form large structures surrounding FAs.
source: It is tempting to speculate that by concentrating KANK1 at the FA rims, talin1 helps to 'nucleate' CMSC assembly, which can then propagate to form large structures surrounding FAs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is presented as a speculative model and illustrated in Figure 6B.

claim: Additional membrane-bound cues, such as the presence of PIP3, can further promote CMSC coalescence by increasing concentration of CMSC players in specific areas of the plasma membrane.
source: Additional membrane-bound cues, such as the presence of PIP3, to which LL5β can bind (Paranavitane et al., 2003), can further promote CMSC coalescence by increasing concentration of CMSC players in specific areas of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated as part of the proposed model with cited knowledge.

claim: The proposed model helps to explain why the CMSC accumulation at the cell periphery is reduced but not abolished when PI3 kinase is inhibited.
source: This model helps to explain why the CMSC accumulation at the cell periphery is reduced but not abolished when PI3 kinase is inhibited (Lansbergen et al., 2006)
evidence: This is stated as an explanation provided by the model with cited knowledge.

claim: The proposed model helps to explain why the clustering of all CMSC components is mutually dependent.
source: and why the clustering of all CMSC components is mutually dependent
evidence: This is stated as an explanation provided by the model.

claim: The proposed model accounts for the ability of the two large and spatially distinct macromolecular assemblies, FAs and CMSCs, to form in close proximity of each other.
source: Most importantly, this model accounts for the mysterious ability of the two large and spatially distinct macromolecular assemblies, FAs and CMSCs, to form in close proximity of each other.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation provided by the model.

claim: Talin not only participates in organizing the actin cytoskeleton but also directly triggers formation of a cortical microtubule-stabilizing macromolecular assembly.
source: To conclude, our study revealed that a mechanosensitive integrin-associated adaptor talin not only participates in organizing the actin cytoskeleton but also directly triggers formation of a cortical microtubule-stabilizing macromolecular assembly
evidence: This is stated as the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The cortical microtubule-stabilizing macromolecular assembly surrounds adhesion sites and controls their formation and dynamics by regulating microtubule-dependent signaling and trafficking.
source: which surrounds adhesion sites and controls their formation and dynamics by regulating microtubule-dependent signaling and trafficking.
evidence: This is stated as the main conclusion of the study.
